quartiers:The Rum quarter.name: The Rum quarter
quartiers:The Rum quarter.teaser: North of the dividing street, a quarter rebuilt in straight lines after the fire of 1874
quartiers:The Rum quarter.story: Officially this is Cumhuriyet Mahallesi, but everyone still calls it the Rum quarter. It is where the island's churches and chapels stand, and its lanes run straight because they were laid out again after the fire of 1874. The tallest house put up in the years just after the fire, built in 1876 by Dimosten Tulmidis, now holds the island museum. Under the bell tower of St Mary the stone houses rise two storeys to wooden bays and shutters, and bougainvillea spills off the walls. On a late October evening most guesthouses are shuttered, and you smell woodsmoke and grilled fish from the few kitchens still lit.
quartiers:The Rum quarter.why: Walk it after the day-trippers have gone, when the straight lanes run empty down to the bell tower.
facts: The 19th-century street grid, the stone houses with wooden bays, and the guesthouses, galleries and wine bars
Early evening, when the lanes empty and the stone takes on the last light
The bell tower of St Mary, and the 1876 Tulmidis house that holds the island museum

quartiers:The Turkish mahalle.name: The Turkish mahalle
quartiers:The Turkish mahalle.teaser: South of the dividing street: the lanes the fire missed, two mosques and a plane-tree fountain
quartiers:The Turkish mahalle.story: Alaybey Mahallesi is the half of town the 1874 fire did not reach, so its lanes still bend the way they did before. Here are the mosques and fountains, where the Rum quarter has its churches. Alaybey Camii is the puzzle: its inscription is lost, and nobody can say for sure who built it or when. The Köprülü Mehmet Paşa mosque is easier to date. The grand vizier had it built around 1657, after the castle was taken back from the Venetians, on the site of an older mosque wrecked during their stay. Nearby, Çınar Çeşme Sokağı, the plane-tree fountain street, smells of almond biscuits and strong tea.
quartiers:The Turkish mahalle.why: Come for the shop counters in the plane-tree lanes by the mosque, open longer into the off-season than the harbour front.
facts: The older, looser street plan, the two mosques and the fountains
Mid-morning, when the shops by the mosque are open and the lanes are in shade

quartiers:The harbour and the castle squ.name: The harbour and the castle square
quartiers:The harbour and the castle squ.teaser: Where the ferry ties up under the castle walls, and the Wednesday stalls set up in the square
quartiers:The harbour and the castle squ.story: The car ferry from Geyikli's Yükyeri quay crosses the strait and docks beneath the castle, and the town opens out from the quay: fishing boats tied up along the harbour wall, tea glasses on the café tables, the wind coming off the water. Behind the quay is Kale Meydanı, the castle square. On Wednesdays it fills with the island's producers: goat cheese, Ezine cheese and jars of tomato jam on trestles under the walls. After dark the castle is floodlit and the masts in the harbour stand out against it. In winter, when most of the registered population has left the island, you share the quay with a few fishermen.
quartiers:The harbour and the castle squ.why: Plan the shore day around a Wednesday, so the castle square is full of island producers when you step off the boat.
facts: The ferry quay, the fishing boats and the castle square
Wednesday morning for the market; after dark for the floodlit walls over the harbour
The view of the walls and the masts together from the end of the quay
The Wednesday Market in the castle square; Nevreste, a few lanes back from the harbour, if it is open (book in summer)

curiosities:Tenedos and the wooden horse.name: Tenedos and the wooden horse
curiosities:Tenedos and the wooden horse.teaser: Virgil hid the Greek fleet behind this island while Troy pulled the horse inside its walls
curiosities:Tenedos and the wooden horse.story: 'Est in conspectu Tenedos', Virgil writes in Book 2 of the Aeneid: there is an island in sight of Troy, famous and rich while Priam's kingdom stood, now only a bay and an unsafe anchorage for ships. Aeneas tells it at Dido's table. The Greeks sail to Tenedos and hide on its empty shore, the Trojans think they have gone, and the horse is pulled into the city. The island's own coins tell another story. From about 420 BC Tenedos struck a double-headed axe on its silver, and beside it, again and again, a bunch of grapes.
curiosities:Tenedos and the wooden horse.why: From the town's west side, look across at the Troad coast: the poem's view, read in reverse.
facts: Look across the strait from the harbour to the Troad shore where Troy stood; the island museum keeps coins among its collections

This is literature, not archaeology: no find places the fleet here. The axe has been read as the emblem of a local god, and Cook (1925) tied the grape-and-axe pair to a Dionysiac cult; the stories of Tenes, the island's founder hero, are later, and Cook argued his name was taken from Tenedos, not the other way round

curiosities:The louse that came late.name: The louse that came late
curiosities:The louse that came late.teaser: 'A pre-phylloxera island', say the guides; the sources found do not back them up
curiosities:The louse that came late.story: The line runs through many Bozcaada guides, ours included: the root louse that wiped out Europe's vineyards in the 19th century only reached the island in the 1940s, so its vines are a pre-phylloxera survival. Searched in English and Turkish in October 2026, the claim has no source. What the record does show is the louse reaching the Ottoman Empire early: in Thrace from 1881, then on the Asian shore of the Bosphorus, at Kızıltoprak, and around Bursa and Aydın from 1885. The state did not formally admit it until 1886. When it reached Tenedos, and whether the vines stand on their own roots today, no source we found records.
curiosities:The louse that came late.why: Ask a grower in the vines whether his stocks are grafted: the honest answer is worth more than the slogan.
facts: At a cellar door ask whether the vines are grafted or on their own roots, and when the old rows were last replanted

The 1940s arrival date and the 'pre-phylloxera island' label appear in guidebooks only. Ottoman sources put the louse in Thrace from 1881 and in Anatolia from 1885; no source found dates its arrival on Bozcaada or says whether today's vines are grafted

curiosities:Left out of the exchange.name: Left out of the exchange
curiosities:Left out of the exchange.teaser: In 1923 the Greek–Turkish population exchange left out two islands, and Tenedos was one of them
curiosities:Left out of the exchange.story: The Treaty of Lausanne returned Imbros and Tenedos to Turkey, three years after the Treaty of Sèvres had given them to Greece, and wrote a promise into Article 14. The islands would have a special local administration with guarantees for their non-Muslim people, and the Greek–Turkish exchange of populations would not apply to them. So while more than a million people elsewhere were moved, Tenedos's Orthodox families stayed, with their vines and their churches. The promise did not hold. The community dwindled over the century that followed, and how far it fell depends on whose figures you take.
curiosities:Left out of the exchange.why: Behind the Rum quarter's bougainvillea is a treaty clause: read it before you walk those lanes.
facts: The church of St Mary and the Rum quarter's lanes, and the Ayazma chapel on 26 July, when the diaspora comes back for the feast

Numbers differ: our old guide had about 5,420 Greeks in 1912 and about 22 by 2000; one 1923 count gives about 1,631 Greeks on Tenedos; another of our pages said 'close to 2,000, now about twenty'. No single official series was found

culture:The castle.name: The castle
culture:The castle.teaser: Mehmet II's 1455 fortress over the harbour, where a 2023 dig reached Late Bronze Age layers
culture:The castle.story: The walls you see are Ottoman. Mehmet II took the island and rebuilt its fortress in 1455, two years after taking Constantinople. Köprülü Mehmet Paşa and later Mahmud II repaired it. Earlier Venetian and Genoese works were pulled down after the 14th-century War of Chioggia. Inside are an outer bailey, an inner citadel and a dry moat on the landward side; from the ramparts you look down on the harbour and across to the Troad. In 2023 the castle was excavated for the first time, and the team under Prof. Turan Takaoğlu found Byzantine, Roman and Late Bronze Age settlement traces below the Ottoman floor.
culture:The castle.why: Walk the ramparts for the one view that holds the harbour, the two quarters and the strait together.
facts: On the harbour, at the head of the castle square

culture:The church of St Mary.name: The church of St Mary
culture:The church of St Mary.teaser: The Rum quarter's church of 1869 rang its bells again after a two-year restoration
culture:The church of St Mary.story: The Kimisis Theotokou, the church of the Dormition of the Virgin, has served the island's Orthodox since 1869. Inside, five Corinthian columns divide a three-aisled nave; outside, the four-storey bell tower stands over the Rum quarter's roofs, and you can see it from most of town. After a two-year restoration the church reopened for worship, and the bells rang for a liturgy led by the Ecumenical Patriarch Bartholomew. The mayor and the island's mufti came, and so did Orthodox families from several countries. Its feast is the Dormition, 15 August.
culture:The church of St Mary.why: Go in quietly on an ordinary morning, when it is still a parish church before it is a sight.
facts: The Rum quarter (Cumhuriyet Mahallesi), under its bell tower

culture:The island museum.name: The island museum
culture:The island museum.teaser: One collector's maps, coins and wine bottles in the tallest house built after the 1874 fire
culture:The island museum.story: The Bozcaada Yerel Tarih Araştırma Merkezi, the Local History Research Centre, fills a house that Dimosten Tulmidis built in 1876. It was the tallest and grandest of the houses put up just after the fire of 1874. The collection is Hakan Gürüney's, an islander who has spent years gathering Bozcaada. There are fossils and archaeological finds, coins, old maps and engravings of Tenedos, island wine bottles, and the household goods of Greek and Turkish families side by side. The building was given over to the collection by a 7 June 2006 protocol with the district governorship. On a windy day it is the quickest way to read the island's layers.
culture:The island museum.why: Look for the old island wine labels: the vineyard history in glass and paper, before you walk the rows.

culture:The windmills.name: The windmills
culture:The windmills.teaser: Rebuilt from islanders' old photographs, the stone mills that once ground the island's wheat
culture:The windmills.story: The island once ground its own wheat in round stone mills along its ridges, and by the late 2010s they were ruins. The district governor İbrahim Gültekin said they had collapsed 50 to 60 years before, from neglect. The district governorship rebuilt them in 2019 from the islanders' memory. Islanders brought out old family photographs to show where each mill had stood, then the sites were cleared and levelled. Two mills, 4 m across and 6.5 m tall, went back up on the island's south side, and a third was under way at the north end. They do not grind. They give the skyline back its old silhouette against the turbines.
culture:The windmills.why: Go up for the silhouette at the end of the day, with the sea and the strait behind the mills.
facts: On the high ground: two on the island's south side, one at the north end

culture:Ayazma chapel and spring.name: Ayazma chapel and spring
culture:Ayazma chapel and spring.teaser: A 1734 chapel under plane trees that opens one day a year, when bread, wine and oil are blessed
culture:Ayazma chapel and spring.story: Ayazma comes from the Greek hagiasma, holy water. The chapel of Aya Paraskevi was built in 1734, attributed to one Manolaki Manolidis, and stands among old plane trees beside a two-spouted fountain that runs all year. For most of the year the door is shut. On 26 July, Saint Paraskevi's day, it opens for the Ayazma Panayırı: islanders and families back from Greece fill the shade, the Metropolitan of Gökçeada and Bozcaada blesses bread, wine and olive oil, and pilgrims light candles and make wishes at the spring. In July 2025 the Ecumenical Patriarch Bartholomew led the service. In October you have the plane trees to yourself.
culture:Ayazma chapel and spring.why: Sit by the running fountain under the planes, the coolest shade on the south coast.
facts: Inland from Ayazma beach on the south coast

walks:Göztepe.name: Göztepe
walks:Göztepe.teaser: The island's high point on foot: vines, pines, the windmills and the islets in one turn of the head
walks:Göztepe.story: Göztepe, the lookout hill, is the top of the island, and the climb is on a path, gentle, through scrub that smells of thyme when the sun is on it. Count about half an hour from the centre. From the top the whole of Bozcaada lies below: the green and rust of the vineyards, the dark pines, the white sails of the rebuilt windmills, the turbine ridge to the west, the islets offshore and the mainland across the strait. The meltem that keeps the vines dry blows hardest up here. By late October the vines below are picked and turning, and a sweater earns its place.
walks:Göztepe.why: Go at the start or the end of the day, when the light lies low across the vineyards.
facts: A gentle footpath to the summit, 192 m by the old guide (not confirmed); the old guide also says no road reaches the top

walks:Polente at sunset.name: Polente at sunset
walks:Polente at sunset.teaser: An hour out along the bare western cape to the 1861 lighthouse, as the turbines turn behind you
walks:Polente at sunset.story: The walk out to Polente is longer than it looks from town: an hour each way, west past the wind farm, over open ground with no tree to stand under. The light at the end has stood on the cape since 1861, a tall white tower of about 30 m. The ridge behind it carries the wind farm, built from around 2000 and now one of the island's landmarks too. The reward comes at the end of the day, when people drive or walk out, sit on the rocks with a beer, and watch the sun drop into the sea beyond the lighthouse. Tuzburnu cove lies just below.
walks:Polente at sunset.why: Stay until the light comes on: the old tower lit against the turbine ridge is the island's evening.
facts: The full width of the island to the western tip
About 1 hour each way on foot
Road and open track, no shade

walks:The vineyard country.name: The vineyard country
walks:The vineyard country.teaser: Low gobelet vines raked by the meltem, from Göztepe's flanks down to the south coast
walks:The vineyard country.story: Between a third and a half of Bozcaada is under vine, and the inland walk is through it. The vines are gobelet bushes, trained low and knuckled close to the dusty ground. They are dry-farmed, and the steady meltem dries the morning damp off the leaves before mildew can take hold. The tracks run open between the rows from below Göztepe to the south coast, Late August into September is the harvest, with the Bağ Bozumu festival at its end. By late October the rows are picked, the leaves go rust and yellow, and the smell of the island's must still hangs around the cellars.
walks:The vineyard country.why: Walk between the rows themselves: the low, wind-shaped vines explain the island's wine better than any glass.
facts: Bozcaada town, taking the tracks inland towards Göztepe
Open-ended: loops of a few kilometres between the rows
